background.definition: Transient synovitis is a self-limited inflammation of the synovium, usually affecting the hip in children.

list.listitem: The average annual incidence in a study of children in the Netherlands was 0.08%, and in a study of Swedish children the incidence was 0.2%.
Boys are affected twice as often as girls.
Generally considered the most common cause of hip pain in children in the United States.
Inflammatory condition of unknown origin, likely triggered by infection.
Several authors have suggested that transient synovitis is caused by a self-limited infection involving the synovial membrane or a postinfectious inflammatory response of the synovium.

Many children with transient synovitis had a recent or concurrent upper respiratory or gastrointestinal viral infection. In one series, an increase in antibodies against rubella, enterovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, or mycoplasma was demonstated in 67 of 80 children with transient synovitis. Some authors have noted a positive throat culture for group A Strep or an elevated ASO titer or both in children with transient synovitis.
Biopsies of the synovial membrane have revealed nonspecific inflammation, and synovial viral cultures have been negative in multiple studies.
While many studies aim to explain the pathophysiology, few advances have been made in this regard.
Transient synovitis usually presents in a previously healthy child between the ages of 3 months and 12 years with leg pain or a limp. C

Transient synovitis is a diagnosis of exclusion; CBC, sedimentation rate or CRP, and radiographic studies help to distinguish this illness from more serious causes of hip pain such as septic arthritis. C
In children with concern for infection MRI or arthrocentesis should be considered. C
Prolonged or recurrent symptoms should prompt an additional work-up to rule out chronic orthopedic or inflammatory conditions that mimic transient synovitis. C

list.listitem: Transient synovitis usually presents in a previously healthy child between the ages of 3 months and 12 years (mean age = 6 years) with leg pain or a limp. It is more common in boys. It has been reported in adults, but rarely.

Symptoms are typically unilateral, with left and right hips affected equally as often. Most children are afebrile or demonstrate only a mild elevation in temperature and usually have a nontoxic appearance.
Internal rotation and adduction of the affected hip are usually limited secondary to pain.

Transient synovitis is a diagnosis of exclusion. WBC, sedimentation rate, and CRP help to distinguish transient synovitis from pyogenic arthritis; a WBC > 14,000 and CRP more than 2.0 mg/dl supports pyogenic arthritis over transient synovitis.

Plain radiographs are typically normal; films can be performed to rule out Legg-Calve-Perthes (LCP) disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), osteomyelitis, and tumor. The American College of Radiology recommends plain radiographs in the evaluation of a limping child (age <5 years).

If radiographs are not diagnostic, and there is concern for infection, a consensus guideline recommends MRI or arthrocentesis. This is also supported by ACR Appropriateness criteria. MRI findings more common in transient synovitis include contralateral (asymptomatic) joint effusions and the absence of signal intensity abnormalities of the bone marrow of the affected side. Ipsilateral joint effusion as well as synovial thickening and enhancment can be seen in both septic arthritis and transient synovitis.
A single ultrasound-guided hip aspiration may be useful for both diagnostic (to rule out septic arthritis) and therapeutic purposes by obtaining fluid for culture.

Ultrasound cannot be used safely to distinguish between septic hip and transient synovitis, because a joint effusion is present in as many as 70% of cases of transient synovitis. However, a point of care ultrasound decision support algorithm may be useful in ruling IN transient synovitis (LR + 4.25).
Use of ultrasound is increasing for diagnosis.

A relationship between transient synovitis and the development of LCP or cox magna remains speculative. Some authors recommend follow-up radiographs 3 to 6 months after the initial episode to rule out these conditions.

When differentiating septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip in children, consider the following 4 criteria: history of fever, unable to bear weight, ESR more than 40 mm/h, and WBC more than 12,000. If all 4 criteria are present, there is a 99.6% chance that the patient has a septic hip. Conversely, if all 4 criteria are negative, then there is a less than 0.2% chance of a septic hip.
When these criteria were applied at a different instituion in a recent retrospective study, the probability of having a septic hip with all 4 criteria present was not quite as high (59%).
Missed diagnosis is more likely to occur in younger children.
Suspect transient synovitis in a child between the ages of 3 and 12 years presenting with hip pain or a limp.
Consider ordering CBC, ESR, and radiographs to differentiate from other causes of hip pain in children.
Consider referral when a septic hip is suspected.
Rest and conservative management are the mainstay for treatment.
Although transient synovitis is a self-limited disease, NSAIDs have been shown to shorten the duration of symptoms significantly. B
Althought transient synovitis is a self-limited disease, NSAIDs have been shown to shorten the duration of symptoms significantly.
One study of 36 patients with transient synovitis found that ibuprofen 10 mg/kg given 3 times daily reduced the duration of symptoms (4.5 vs 2.0 days, P = .05).

Consider hospitalization of patients when presenting with severe pain and muscle spasm requiring traction and narcotic analgesia, or while awaiting synovial culture results in a toxic-appearing child.

A retrospective cohort study showed marked symptom improvement with a single ultrasound-guided aspiration of the hip. Aspiration also improves accuracy of diagnosis to detect intracapsular effusion and rapid distinction from septic arthritis with synovial fluid analysis.
Transient synovitis usually has a benign course, and adverse outcomes are rare. C
The recurrence rate is 4% to 17%, but even then the course is usually benign.
Consider follow-up for at least 6 months and repeating radiographs after the initial episode to exclude Legg-Calve-Perthes.

Adverse outcomes include limited range of motion (rate <10%) and coxa magna with mild degenerative changes of the femoral head (rate 0% to 32.1%) often within the first year following transient synovitis.
